title: Franconian Squares, Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl and the Ries

bestPeriod.note: Late September gives warm stone, thin crowds and the first Federweisser; December is beautiful but the Reiterlesmarkt fills Rothenburg.

summary: Three walled Franconian towns in seven days, Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl and Nördlingen, with market mornings, Riemenschneider altars and only two moves.
hook: Three towns that never grew. Rothenburg kept its walls because it went broke after 1631, Dinkelsbühl because nobody bothered to knock them down, and Nördlingen because it sits in a meteorite crater with nowhere to sprawl. This week walks all three at the speed of a market morning, with two relocations in seven days and a great deal of sitting on squares.

snapshot.Base(s): Rothenburg ob der Tauber (3 nights) · Dinkelsbühl (2) · Nördlingen (2)
snapshot.Total Distance / Terrain: Approx. 95 km of driving in total; 45-55 km walked over the week; flat cobbles, wall parapets, one gentle river valley
snapshot.Getting There: Fly Nürnberg (NUE); train to Steinach (b Rothenburg) and the branch line in, or rent a car at the airport
snapshot.Who It Suits: Slow travellers, families with children over six, anyone who wants medieval Germany without a coach-park itinerary

itinerary.title: Arrival and the first circuit of the wall
itinerary.morning: Land at Nürnberg, collect the car, and drive the 90 km southwest to Rothenburg, about 1h10 on the A6 and B25. Leave the car outside the walls; the Altstadt is closed to through traffic and hotel guests get a permit for loading only. Park P1 (Schwäbsche Hall Straße) or P5 by the Bahnhof, approx. €5-7 per day.
itinerary.afternoon: Do nothing ambitious. Walk the covered parapet of the Stadtmauer, joined at the Rödertor and followed anticlockwise, roughly 2.5 km of the 4 km circuit is walkable, free, and mostly empty after 17:00. Come down at the Klingentor, cut through to the Marktplatz, and look at the Rathaus: Gothic tower behind a Renaissance front by Leonhard Weidmann, 1572.
itinerary.evening: The Plönlein, the fork where Untere Schmiedgasse splits, with the yellow house wedged between the Kobolzeller Tor and the Siebersturm, is unbearable at noon and beautiful at 19:30. Then dinner in the Herrngasse end of town, and the Nachtwächter round: the night watchman leaves the Rathaus arcade on the Marktplatz at 20:00 in English, April to December, approx. €10, no booking, just turn up.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Rothenburg). Walking: 5 km. Transfer: 1h10 by car from NUE.

itinerary.title: Creglingen, a Riemenschneider altar and a museum of thimbles
itinerary.morning: A late breakfast, then 20 km north up the Tauber to Creglingen, 25 minutes on the L1020 through Detwang and Bettwar. The Herrgottskirche stands alone in a field 2 km south of the village. Inside is Tilman Riemenschneider's Marienaltar, carved around 1505-10 in limewood and never painted; in the second half of the morning the south windows put light straight onto it. Approx. €4.
itinerary.afternoon: Fifty metres away, the Fingerhutmuseum, a genuine one-room obsession, thimbles from Roman bronze to 19th-century Creglingen porcelain, built on the town's own thimble-making industry. Approx. €3. Afterwards, the Jüdisches Museum Creglingen in the old village of Archshofen, or simply the walk along the Tauber meadows.
itinerary.evening: Back to Rothenburg by 18:00. Eat early, then drop through the Kobolzeller Tor into the Burggarten for the last light over the Taubertal, this is the one view in town that turns gold rather than orange.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Rothenburg, Creglingen). Walking: 6 km. Transfer: 45 min driving, return.

itinerary.title: Market morning, craftsmen's house, and the Tauber loop
itinerary.morning: Market day. Rothenburg's Wochenmarkt sets up on the Marktplatz on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, usually from about 07:00 until 12:30, Franconian asparagus in May, Zwetschgen and Bamberger Hörnla potatoes in September, plus a cheese van and a smoked-fish stall. Buy lunch here, not in a restaurant.
itinerary.afternoon: The Alt-Rothenburger Handwerkerhaus at Alter Stadtgraben 26 is a 700-year-old artisans' house left as its coopers, weavers, dyers, potters and shoemakers used it, eleven rooms, original workbenches, approx. €3.50. Then walk down through the Kobolzeller gate to the Doppelbrücke, the double-decked stone bridge over the Tauber, past the Topplerschlösschen of 1388 to Detwang, whose village church holds a second Riemenschneider, the Kreuzaltar, older and rougher than the Creglingen one. It is 1.5 km down and 1.5 km back up, all on a made path.
itinerary.evening: Schneeballen, the fist-sized fried pastry knot, is Rothenburg's edible cliché, and the honest way to eat one is at a working bakery on Untere Schmiedgasse rather than a souvenir shop. One is enough for two people.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 1 (Rothenburg + Detwang). Walking: 8 km. Transfer: none.

itinerary.title: South to Dinkelsbühl
itinerary.morning: An unhurried morning: coffee on the Marktplatz, the Rathausturm if the weather is clear (220 steep steps and a ladder at the top, approx. €2.50, best before 11:00), then load the car.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 47 km south on the B25, the old Romantic Road alignment through Schillingsfürst and Feuchtwangen, about 50 minutes. Check in inside Dinkelsbühl's walls and walk the Weinmarkt, the town's long spine of a square: the Deutsches Haus of 1440 with its carved timber front, the Schranne, and the Münster St. Georg at the end, one of the purest late-Gothic hall churches in southern Germany, its nave startlingly white.
itinerary.evening: Dinkelsbühl's night watchman walks nightly at 21:00 from the Münster, April to October, in German, singing rather than lecturing, free, tip the horn. Before that, the Rothenburger Weiher on the town's east side gives the whole wall reflected in water at dusk.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: 50 min / 47 km.

itinerary.title: Dinkelsbühl slowly, and Feuchtwangen's cloister
itinerary.morning: Market morning again, Dinkelsbühl's weekly market usually runs Wednesday and Saturday mornings from about 07:30 to 12:30 on the Altrathausplatz. Then the Haus der Geschichte in the old town hall, which does an honest job on the Thirty Years' War and the Kinderzeche, the children's festival held every third weekend of July since 1897.
itinerary.afternoon: Optional 25 km north to Feuchtwangen for the Romanesque Kreuzgang, a cloister used as an open-air theatre every summer by the Kreuzgangspiele, and the Fränkisches Museum's peasant furniture and painted cupboards. Or skip the car entirely and walk the full ring of Dinkelsbühl's wall from the outside: 2.5 km, sixteen towers, no crowds, wholly flat.
itinerary.evening: Wine on the Weinmarkt. Franconia's dry Silvaner in the squat Bocksbeutel is the local pour and it goes with Schäufele, roast pork shoulder, better than beer does.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Dinkelsbühl, Feuchtwangen). Walking: 7 km. Transfer: 45 min driving, return.

itinerary.title: Into the crater: Nördlingen
itinerary.morning: A long breakfast, then 32 km south on the B25 to Nördlingen, about 35 minutes. You cross the crater rim near Maihingen without noticing it, a 15-million-year-old impact basin 25 km wide, which is why the fields go suddenly flat.
itinerary.afternoon: Nördlingen is the only town in Germany with a completely walkable circular wall: 2.6 km, covered for most of its length, five gates, eleven towers, free and open all day. Do the whole ring, then the Rieskrater-Museum in the Klösterle barn of 1503, which explains the impact and displays a lunar sample lent by NASA, approx. €4.50.
itinerary.evening: Climb the Daniel, the 90 m tower of St.-Georgs-Kirche, 350 steps, approx. €5. The tower keeper still lives up there and calls "So, G'sell, so" across the roofs on the half hour between 22:00 and midnight. From the top the crater rim is a visible ring on the horizon.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Dinkelsbühl, Nördlingen). Walking: 6 km. Transfer: 35 min / 32 km.

itinerary.title: Market on the Marktplatz, then Harburg
itinerary.morning: Nördlingen's weekly market fills the Marktplatz on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, usually 07:00-12:30, in front of the Rathaus with its outdoor stone staircase of 1618. Ries onion, Swabian Spätzle flour, farm eggs. Eat breakfast off the stalls sitting on the Rathaus steps.
itinerary.afternoon: Twelve kilometres south, Schloss Harburg sits over the Wörnitz gorge, one of the oldest and least restored castles in southern Germany, with a real dungeon tower and a courtyard you can loiter in. Approx. €8 with a tour.
itinerary.evening: Return the car at Nürnberg (1h15 via the B25/A6) or take the train from Nördlingen via Donauwörth. If you have the evening, spend it back on the Nördlingen Marktplatz, it empties by 19:00 and the town belongs to its 20,000 residents again.
itinerary.dayStats: Towns: 2 (Nördlingen, Harburg). Walking: 4 km. Transfer: 25 min to Harburg; 1h15 to NUE.

accommodationStrategy.name: Burg-Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Fifteen rooms built into the town wall at Klostergasse, with a terrace that hangs directly over the Tauber valley. It is inside the pedestrian zone, so you unload with a permit and then forget the car for three days, which is the whole point of basing here. Ask for a valley-side room; the town-side ones face a quiet lane but see nothing.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three months ahead for September; six for December.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel Deutsches Haus
accommodationStrategy.description: The 1440 timber facade on the Weinmarkt is the most photographed building in town and the rooms behind it are plain, comfortable and quiet after the square empties at 22:00. You are thirty seconds from the night watchman's start point and the Saturday market, and the kitchen serves Franconian standards late by small-town standards.
accommodationStrategy.booking: two months ahead; avoid the Kinderzeche weekend in July unless that is the point.

accommodationStrategy.name: Hotel-Restaurant Klosterhof
accommodationStrategy.description: A calm, family-run house a few minutes' walk inside the wall, with parking on site, important, because Nördlingen's centre is tight and market mornings take the Marktplatz spaces. Good base for a two-night finish: you can walk the whole wall from the door and be at the Daniel in five minutes.
accommodationStrategy.booking: one month ahead outside festival dates.

logistics.emergency: 112 for everything across Germany; 110 for police. Pharmacies rotate a night service, the roster is posted in every Apotheke window as the *Notdienst*.
logistics.bookingWindows: The night watchman tours take no reservations. Restaurant tables inside Rothenburg's walls need a call by mid-afternoon in season. December accommodation in Rothenburg goes six to nine months out.

other.label: Emergencies
other.text: 112 for everything across Germany; 110 for police. Pharmacies rotate a night service, the roster is posted in every Apotheke window as the *Notdienst*.

other.label: Cash still matters
other.text: Franconian market stalls, small bakeries, church donation boxes and most tower climbs are cash-only. Carry €80-100 in small notes; there is an ATM on the Rothenburg Marktplatz and one on Dinkelsbühl's Segringer Straße.

other.label: The opening-hour trap
other.text: Small-town Germany closes at 18:00 on weekdays and around 14:00 on Saturdays, and shuts entirely on Sundays, bakeries excepted, which usually open Sunday morning for two or three hours. Buy anything you need on Saturday morning.

other.label: Monday closures
other.text: Museums in all three towns commonly close on Mondays outside high summer. The wall walks, churches and squares never do, which is why Day 1 and Day 4 are built around walls rather than exhibits.

other.label: Driving and parking
other.text: No environmental zone (Umweltplakette) applies in these towns, unlike Nürnberg city centre, if you detour into Nürnberg you need the green sticker. All three old towns restrict access; use the marked P lots outside the gates and pay at the machine.

other.label: Car-free version
other.text: Rothenburg is reachable by train via Steinach; Nördlingen sits on the Aalen-Donauwörth line. Dinkelsbühl has no railway at all, regional buses connect it to Rothenburg and Nördlingen but run a handful of times a day and thin out badly on Sundays. If you refuse to drive, spend four nights in Rothenburg and three in Nördlingen and treat Dinkelsbühl as a weekday bus excursion.

other.label: Drones
other.text: are effectively unusable over these old towns: the walls, towers and dense residential roofs put you inside flight restrictions and within earshot of everybody.

proTips: Rothenburg empties between 17:30 and 09:30. Coach groups arrive around 10:00 and are gone by 16:30, stay inside the walls and you get the Plönlein, the Marktplatz and the wall walk to yourself twice a day.
Walk the Rothenburg wall clockwise from the Rödertor in the evening; the low sun is then behind you and the Taubertal side is lit rather than backlit.
The Herrgottskirche altar in Creglingen is unlit by design. Go between 11:00 and 13:00, when daylight from the south windows falls across the carving, much better than any spotlight.
In Nördlingen, do the wall circuit before the Daniel climb. From the parapet you learn the town's shape; from the tower you then read the crater rim, which otherwise looks like ordinary hills.
Buy Franconian wine at the market stalls, not in the souvenir shops on Herrngasse, the same growers from the Tauber valley sell direct, roughly a third cheaper.
Order Schneeballen fresh from a bakery counter rather than pre-bagged. They stale within a day and the vacuum-packed ones on the tourist streets are often weeks old.
If you are here on a Wednesday or Saturday, plan the day around the market and eat your main meal at midday. Kitchens in all three towns do their best work at lunch.
Schloss Harburg is 12 km from Nördlingen and almost nobody on the Romantic Road stops there. Go in the last hour before closing.

packingNotes: Shoes with real grip: Franconian cobbles are rounded river stone, slick after rain, and the wall parapets have worn stone steps.
A compact rain shell, May and September both deliver 20-minute downpours with no warning.
A torch or phone light for the Daniel stair and the Rothenburg wall towers, which are unlit.
€100 in coins and small notes for markets, church boxes and tower turnstiles.
Binoculars: the Riemenschneider altars are roped off at three metres and the detail is the whole point.
A folding tote for market shopping, no stall in Germany gives you a bag.
One layer warmer than you expect for evenings; the Ries and the Tauber valley both drop sharply after sunset in autumn.
A refillable bottle: public fountains on the Marktplatz in Rothenburg and Nördlingen run drinking water unless posted *kein Trinkwasser*.
whatCouldGoWrong: **You arrive on a Monday and everything is shut.** Fallback: the wall circuits, all three parish churches and the market squares are open daily and free. Shift museum days to Tuesday and Wednesday.
**Rothenburg is overwhelming at midday.** If the crowd ruins it, walk out through the Kobolzeller gate to Detwang, twenty minutes down the valley and you will meet six people instead of six hundred.

**The Dinkelsbühl bus doesn't run on Sunday.** If you are car-free and get stranded, taxis operate between Dinkelsbühl and Ansbach or Nördlingen at roughly €70-90; book a day ahead through your hotel.
**December crowds and prices.** Rothenburg's Reiterlesmarkt triples room rates and fills the lanes. If you want Advent, base in Dinkelsbühl or Nördlingen and day-trip in on a weekday morning.

**Bad weather kills the tower climbs.** The Daniel and the Rathausturm close in high wind or ice. Substitute the Rieskrater-Museum, the Handwerkerhaus and a long lunch, both towns are built for weather.
